name: Tim Sweeney
milestone_by_age_26: Founded Epic MegaGames (originally Potomac Computer Systems) and released ZZT, a text-based adventure game with a built-in editor and scripting language, in early 1991 at age 20, launching what would become Epic Games.
early_history_summary: Sweeney taught himself programming starting at age 11 on an Apple II, spending an estimated 10,000+ hours between ages 11 and 15 creating dozens of games and programs shared via BBSes. He attended the University of Maryland for mechanical engineering while developing ZZT part-time over nine months, releasing it in early 1991 and founding Epic MegaGames from his parents' basement.
family_context_summary: Born in 1970 and raised in Potomac, Maryland, the youngest of three brothers. His father was a cartographer for the US government and his mother took care of the family. His eldest brother worked at a startup in California and introduced him to programming on IBM PCs, later giving him an Apple II.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a US government cartographer; no direct tech industry connection. Older brother provided critical early access to computers and programming instruction, catalyzing Sweeney's self-education.
primary_early_advantage_tags: self-taught programming, BBS learning, Apple II, shareware distribution, 10000 hours, brother mentorship
evidence_summary: Sweeney spent over 10,000 hours self-teaching programming between ages 11 and 15 on an Apple II, creating dozens of games and hundreds of programs. His older brother provided initial access to computers and programming instruction, but Sweeney was largely self-taught through BBSes and experimentation. He founded Epic MegaGames from his parents' basement in 1991 at age 20, releasing ZZT as a shareware title. The shareware distribution model of the early 1990s and the PC gaming wave provided the structural context for his breakout. No significant family financial or domain advantages are documented beyond a middle-class upbringing and his brother's early mentorship.
starting_point: Born in 1970 in Potomac, Maryland to a middle-class family; father was a US government cartographer, mother a homemaker; youngest of three brothers.
current_position: Founder and CEO of Epic Games; net worth estimated at ~$7.6-9.6 billion (Forbes/Bloomberg, 2025); resides in Cary, North Carolina.

trajectory.event: Founded Epic MegaGames (originally Potomac Computer Systems) and released ZZT, a shareware text-based adventure game with built-in editor, from his parents' basement.
Released Unreal, the first game powered by Unreal Engine, establishing Epic as a major game engine provider.
Unreal Engine 3 launched, adopted by hundreds of studios and becoming the industry-standard game engine for a generation.
Tencent acquired a ~40% stake in Epic Games, providing capital for expansion.
Fortnite launched in early access, becoming one of the highest-grossing video games of all time with 650+ million registered players.
Epic Games valued at $31.5 billion after $2 billion funding round from Sony and LEGO parent company.

name: Andrew Appel
milestone_by_age_26: Completed Ph.D. in computer science at Carnegie Mellon University in 1985 at age 25 and co-created Rog-O-Matic, an early AI belligerent expert system that autonomously played the game Rogue, presented at CSCSI in 1984.
early_history_summary: Appel graduated summa cum laude with an A.B. in physics from Princeton in 1981, completing a senior thesis on galaxy clustering under Nobel laureate James Peebles. At CMU he co-developed Rog-O-Matic (1981-1984), one of the earliest autonomous game-playing AI systems, and completed his Ph.D. on semantics-directed compilers in 1985. He joined Princeton as assistant professor in 1986.
family_context_summary: Son of Kenneth Appel, the mathematician who proved the Four Color Theorem in 1976 with Wolfgang Haken at the University of Illinois. Father was a tenured mathematics professor, providing an academic household environment.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father Kenneth Appel was a renowned mathematician whose proof of the Four Color Theorem was the first major theorem proved with computer assistance, directly connecting mathematics and computing in the family environment.
primary_early_advantage_tags: mathematician father, Four Color Theorem, Princeton, CMU, academic pipeline, Rog-O-Matic
evidence_summary: Appel grew up in the household of Kenneth Appel, the mathematician who proved the Four Color Theorem, providing deep exposure to mathematics and computing from an early age. He graduated summa cum laude in physics from Princeton and earned his Ph.D. at CMU by age 25, co-creating Rog-O-Matic along the way. The elite academic pipeline from Princeton to CMU, combined with his father's domain expertise in mathematical computing, positioned him at the frontier of compiler and programming language research. His career trajectory from assistant professor at Princeton to department chair and ACM Fellow reflects sustained depth in a scarce intellectual domain.
starting_point: Born in 1960 to Kenneth Appel, a mathematics professor who would prove the Four Color Theorem in 1976, providing an academic household immersed in mathematics and early computing.
current_position: Eugene Higgins Professor Emeritus of Computer Science at Princeton University; Visiting Professor at Cornell University; ACM Fellow.

trajectory.event: Graduated summa cum laude with an A.B. in physics from Princeton University, completing a senior thesis under Nobel laureate James Peebles.
Co-authored Rog-O-Matic paper presented at the CSCSI conference, describing an autonomous AI system that played the game Rogue.
Completed Ph.D. in computer science at Carnegie Mellon University with a thesis on semantics-directed compilers.
Joined Princeton University as assistant professor of computer science.
Named a Fellow of the Association for Computing Machinery for research in programming languages and compilers.
Became chair of Princeton's Computer Science Department, serving until 2015.

By age 26 he was a graduate student at MIT working on his doctorate under Marvin Minsky, which while notable does not constitute a material, independently verifiable milestone in the rubric's sense.

name: Ingo Molnar
milestone_by_age_26: Co-developed and announced the Linux software RAID-1 driver in December 1996 at age 23, and the RAID-1/4/5 driver for Linux 2.0.30 in July 1997 at age 24, making significant contributions to the Linux kernel before age 26.
early_history_summary: Molnar first heard about Linux around 1993 and became hooked on kernel development in 1995 after purchasing the 'Linux Kernel Internals' book, installing Linux solely to study the kernel source. He began contributing to the Linux kernel in 1995 at age 22, developing software RAID support with Miguel de Icaza and Gadi Oxman, and announcing RAID-1 for Linux in December 1996.
family_context_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. Molnar is Hungarian and studied at Eotvos Lorand University.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Linux kernel, open source, LKML, software RAID, self-taught kernel development
evidence_summary: Molnar became fascinated with the Linux kernel source code in 1995 at age 22, installing Linux solely to study it. Within a year he was co-developing software RAID support for the kernel, announcing RAID-1 in December 1996 and RAID-1/4/5 in July 1997. His self-driven immersion in kernel internals, facilitated by the Linux Kernel Mailing List community and collaboration with Miguel de Icaza and Gadi Oxman, enabled rapid contributions to a scarce domain. No family or financial advantages are documented; his breakthrough came from intense self-study and the open source collaboration model.
starting_point: Born in 1973 in Hungary; studied at Eotvos Lorand University. Family background not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Linux kernel developer employed by Red Hat; known for the Completely Fair Scheduler, O(1) scheduler, and PREEMPT_RT real-time patch set.

trajectory.event: Began contributing to the Linux kernel after installing Linux specifically to study the kernel source code.
Co-developed and announced the Linux software RAID-1 driver with Miguel de Icaza.
Released the software RAID-1/4/5 driver for Linux 2.0.30, adding RAID-4 and RAID-5 support.
O(1) scheduler merged into the Linux 2.5 development kernel, a major performance improvement.
Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS) replaced the Linux process scheduler in Linux 2.6.23.
Employed by Red Hat as a kernel developer, continuing work on real-time preemption (PREEMPT_RT).

name: Tracy Chou
milestone_by_age_26: Joined Quora as the 4th/5th employee in 2010 at age 23, then joined Pinterest in October 2011 as one of the first ~10 employees at age 24, becoming a foundational engineer at two breakout consumer tech companies before age 26.
early_history_summary: Chou grew up in Silicon Valley as the daughter of two Taiwanese computer scientists with PhDs. She attended St. Francis High School in Mountain View, then Stanford University, earning a B.S. in electrical engineering and an M.S. in computer science with a specialization in machine learning and AI. She interned at Google and Facebook during college and was a Terman Scholar and Mayfield Fellow at Stanford. In 2010 she joined Quora as one of its first employees, then moved to Pinterest in 2011.
family_context_summary: Daughter of Taiwanese computer scientists who immigrated to Silicon Valley; both parents held CS PhDs and worked as software engineers. She grew up in Mountain View, the heart of Silicon Valley, spending afternoons at her parents' startup.
parent_family_domain_summary: Both parents were computer scientists with PhDs who worked as software engineers in Silicon Valley, providing direct domain expertise, early tech exposure, and an immersive environment for a future software engineer.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Silicon Valley native, Stanford, tech parents, Google/Facebook internships, Mayfield Fellow, Quora, Pinterest
evidence_summary: Chou was born into the Silicon Valley ecosystem: both parents were Taiwanese computer scientists with PhDs who worked as software engineers, and she grew up in Mountain View spending time at her parents' startup. She attended Stanford for her B.S. and M.S., interned at Google and Facebook, and was a Terman Scholar and Mayfield Fellow. At age 23 she joined Quora as its 4th/5th employee and at 24 joined Pinterest as one of its first 10 employees. Her trajectory reflects deep institutional ecosystem acceleration — born at the frontier, educated at the elite institution, and embedded in high-signal networks from childhood. She also faced sexism in tech, which later catalyzed her diversity advocacy work.
starting_point: Born in 1987 in Silicon Valley to Taiwanese immigrant parents, both computer scientists with PhDs who worked as software engineers; grew up in Mountain View surrounded by tech culture.
current_position: Founder and CEO of Block Party (acquired by DeleteMe), an online safety and anti-harassment platform; joining Anthropic as Member of Technical Staff; based in San Francisco.

trajectory.event: Joined Quora as the 4th/5th employee, working as an early engineer at the then-fledgling Q&A startup.

Founded Block Party, a consumer tool for online safety, privacy, and anti-harassment (later acquired by DeleteMe).
Announced joining Anthropic as a Member of Technical Staff.

name: David R. Brown (engineer)
milestone_by_age_26: Selected as one of 28 students for the seminal Moore School Lectures in 1946 at age 22, then enlisted by Jay Forrester in 1947 at age 23 to lead the Electrical Engineering Division of Project Whirlwind at MIT, where he led Group 63 in developing and installing the ferrite magnetic core memory for one of the first large-scale digital computers.
early_history_summary: Brown earned an electrical engineering degree from the University of Washington and married in 1944. In 1946 he began graduate studies at MIT and was selected as one of 28 students for the Moore School Lectures, the seminal lecture series that introduced the revolutionary potential of digital computers. In 1947, Jay Forrester enlisted him for Project Whirlwind, placing him in charge of the Electrical Engineering Division and as group leader for Group 63 (Magnetic Materials), which developed the ferrite magnetic core memory.
family_context_summary: Born on October 31, 1923 in Los Angeles, California. Father Gilbert Brown was a newspaper reporter, critic, and editor who moved the family to Seattle for a job at the Seattle Post-Intelligencer. Brown attended Queen Anne High School and the University of Washington.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a newspaper reporter, critic, and editor; no direct connection to engineering or computing. The family was working-to-middle class, with no documented tech domain advantage.
primary_early_advantage_tags: MIT, Moore School Lectures, Project Whirlwind, Jay Forrester, ferrite core memory, early computing
evidence_summary: Brown was born to a newspaper reporter father in Los Angeles and raised in Seattle, with no family connection to computing. His trajectory changed when he enrolled at MIT for graduate studies in 1946 and was selected as one of only 28 students for the Moore School Lectures — the foundational lecture series in digital computing. At age 23, Jay Forrester enlisted him to lead the Electrical Engineering Division of Project Whirlwind, where he led Group 63 in developing the ferrite magnetic core memory, a foundational technology for digital computing. His advantages were entirely institutional: MIT and the Moore School Lectures placed him at the absolute frontier of computing in the 1940s, with access to one of the first large-scale computers and mentorship from the field's pioneers.
starting_point: Born on October 31, 1923 in Los Angeles, California to Gilbert Brown, a newspaper reporter and editor, and Blanche Brown; family moved to Seattle where he attended the University of Washington for electrical engineering.
current_position: Died on April 16, 2016 at age 92 in Redwood City, California; final roles included manager of the Computer Techniques Laboratory at SRI International and IEEE Life Fellow.

trajectory.event: Graduated from the University of Washington with an electrical engineering degree and married Sarah Jane England.
Began graduate studies at MIT and was selected as one of 28 students for the seminal Moore School Lectures on digital computing.
Enlisted by Jay Forrester to lead the Electrical Engineering Division of Project Whirlwind at MIT, heading Group 63 which developed the ferrite magnetic core memory.
Transitioned to work on the SAGE computer defense system at MIT Lincoln Laboratory, becoming the first manager of the Advanced Development Group.
Joined SRI International as manager of the Computer Techniques Laboratory, later heading the Information Science Laboratory and doing early work on AI and robotics.
Inducted into the SRI International Hall of Fame for exceptional contributions to the enduring success of SRI.
Died on April 16, 2016 in Redwood City, California.

name: Yehuda Katz
category: Open source developer, web framework creator

early_history_summary: Katz began his career as a print designer before transitioning to programming around 2005 through Ruby on Rails, which he credits with showing him he could be a programmer. He became a jQuery core team member in 2005, joined Engine Yard in January 2008 as its first engineering hire, became the lead developer and maintainer of Merb, released Merb 1.0 in October 2008, and joined the Rails core team in 2008, orchestrating the Merb-Rails merger announced in December 2008.
family_context_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. Katz attended Brooklyn College from 2002 to 2006 and was a print designer before transitioning to programming.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources; no evidence of parental tech or programming background. Katz came from a design background rather than a technical one.
primary_early_advantage_tags: open source communities, jQuery, Rails, Merb, web frameworks, career transition, Engine Yard
evidence_summary: Katz transitioned from print designer to programmer around 2005 at age 22, learning through Ruby on Rails and quickly becoming a jQuery core team member. Within three years he joined Engine Yard as its first engineering hire, became the lead developer of Merb, released Merb 1.0, and joined the Rails core team, all by age 25. His rapid rise was driven by deep immersion in open source communities — jQuery, Rails, and Merb — which served as repeatable channels for learning, reputation-building, and distribution. He collaborated with Ezra Zygmuntowicz on Merb and later co-created Ember.js. No family, financial, or institutional advantages are documented; his breakthrough came from the open source platform-native compounding model and a career-transition-driven urgency.
starting_point: Born in 1983; attended Brooklyn College (2002-2006); began career as a print designer before self-teaching programming through Ruby on Rails around 2005. Family background not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Co-founder and CTO of Tilde Inc (Portland, OR), co-creator of Ember.js and Skylight; core team member emeritus of jQuery, Rails, and Rust; W3C TAG and ECMA TC39 committee member.

trajectory.event: Transitioned from print designer to programmer and became a jQuery core team member, learning web development through Ruby on Rails.
Joined Engine Yard as its first engineering hire; became lead developer of Merb and released Merb 1.0 in October.
Became a Ruby on Rails core team member and announced the Merb-Rails merger in December, consolidating the Ruby web framework ecosystem.
Rails 3.0 released in August, incorporating the Merb architecture that Katz had developed.
Co-founded Tilde Inc. and began developing Ember.js, a JavaScript framework for ambitious web applications.
Ember.js gained widespread enterprise adoption; Katz continued as a leader in the JavaScript and web standards communities.
